cards.front: What is the difference between composition and inheritance?
cards.back: Composition puts an existing object inside the new class; inheritance makes the new class a type of the old one
cards.extra: Composition reuses behaviour without accepting the base type's interface. Inheritance reuses it and becomes substitutable for the base.
cards.example:
class Engine { void start() { } }
class Car { private final Engine e = new Engine(); void start() { e.start(); } }  // has-a: composition
class RaceCar extends Car { }  // is-a: inheritance

cards.front: When should you prefer composition to inheritance?
cards.back: When the relationship is has-a, or when you want to reuse code without committing to the base type's interface
cards.extra: Inheritance is a permanent, structural claim: everything public in the base becomes part of your API. Composition can be changed later, even at runtime.
cards.example:
class Helper { int work() { return 1; } }
class User { private final Helper h = new Helper(); int run() { return h.work(); } }  // has-a reuse; no base-type interface promised

cards.front: How does an object become a String when you concatenate it?
cards.extra: Every object has one, inherited from Object. Overriding it is what turns Dog@1b6d3586 into something readable in logs.
cards.example:
class Thing { public String toString() { return "Thing!"; } }
class Demo { void run() { System.out.println("value: " + new Thing()); } }  // compiler inserts toString(): value: Thing!

cards.front: Object references inside a new class start as what?
cards.extra: You must attach an object before use: at the declaration, in the constructor, lazily on demand, or in an instance initialisation block.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class Holder { String label; int count; boolean ready; }
class Demo { void run() { Holder h = new Holder(); System.out.println(h.label + "," + h.count + "," + h.ready); } }  // null,0,false

cards.back: Creating the object only when it is first needed, not in the constructor
cards.extra: It avoids paying for objects that may never be used, and it is the usual answer for expensive or optional collaborators.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class Helper { }
class Lazy { Helper h; Helper get() { if (h == null) h = new Helper(); return h; } }  // created on first call, not in the constructor

cards.front: What does final on a class prevent?
cards.extra: String and the wrapper classes are final. It is how a class promises its behaviour cannot be altered by subclassing.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword
cards.example:
final class Fixed { int n = 1; }
// class Sub extends Fixed { }  // compile error: a final class cannot be extended

cards.front: What is the trap with final and private methods?
cards.back: A private method cannot be overridden, so final on it is redundant
cards.extra: Private methods are invisible to subclasses, so the compiler binds them statically. Any "override" is just a new, unrelated method.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword
cards.example:
class Parent { private final void secret() { } }
class Child extends Parent { private void secret() { } }  // a new method, not an override; final was redundant
